    Central Oregon Civic Assembly on AI

    This is the shared reading library for delegates to the Central Oregon Civic Assembly on AI. Use it to get oriented on public engagement and AI decisions in Deschutes, Crook, and Jefferson counties before the assembly, and to look things up during it.

    Start reading → Ask a question

    Introduction & overview

    What are we talking about?

    The guiding question: “How should the people of Central Oregon be involved in local and state decisions related to AI technology and infrastructure?”

    This question came through thorough engagement with the Central Oregon community. Polling and conversations across Central Oregon in spring 2026 surfaced two priorities: a desire for greater community involvement in decision-making, and AI technology and infrastructure as a topic of particular concern. The Civic Assembly on AI brings the two together.

    Artificial intelligence is a rapidly developing technology that will likely have far-reaching consequences for our personal lives, the economy, and more. Whether you are optimistic, pessimistic, or unsure about what a future with more AI will bring, many people agree that the people of Central Oregon will be well served by figuring out how the public can best engage on these issues. That matters before decisions are made that are likely to affect land and other natural resources, the education of Central Oregon’s youth and future workforce, our towns, our ability to work and do business, and more.

    Through these deliberations, we will think together about what we want our future to be, what accountability by government to the public means and requires, and what specific steps we can take as voters and taxpayers to ensure Central Oregon’s elected representatives are prepared to shepherd AI-related changes in a direction that enables the pursuit of life, liberty, and happiness for everyone.

    A note for delegates. As a Civic Assembly delegate, you will arrive with perspectives about AI that may differ from those around you. Some may support new AI data centers; others may oppose them. These are important issues, but the Assembly is not designed to settle those particular debates.

    Instead, delegates will consider how the people of Central Oregon can have a meaningful voice in decisions about AI, whether those decisions are made by local or state governments, school districts, or other institutions. AI offers one focused, timely topic within the much larger universe of decisions that shape our communities. In the end, delegates will offer a community-centered perspective on how to engage and involve residents when local and state decisions related to AI are made.

    How to use these learning materials

    In preparation for this Civic Assembly, the Central Oregon Civic Action Project engaged with a wide range of public servants, community-based organizations, community engagement experts, and more.

    The materials are divided into a few key sections:

    • AI-related decisions, laying out the different kinds of decisions that our state and local governments are making related to AI
    • Public engagement, covering how and when the public is able to influence these decisions
    • Case studies on what has worked for other places, and what could still be better

    You are not expected to read every word of these materials. Instead, we have broken them up based on the smaller questions they can help you answer. Feel free to jump around to the different questions and sections.

    During the Assembly, live presentations and discussions will further support shared understanding. Assembly staff will be able to help find answers to any questions that come up during the discussions, and local subject-matter experts will also be there to answer more specific questions.

    If you have any questions before then, please add them to the Question Board, where they may also be shared with other delegates to support broader learning. You can also email Delegate Concierge Mickie Derting directly at mickie@cocap.us.

    What are we talking about when we say “AI”?

    Key points

    • AI is a broad term for computer systems that can perform tasks with human-like intelligence, like understanding language or recognizing images.
    • Unlike traditional software, modern AI systems “learn” patterns from data, and in some cases can complete tasks with minimal human supervision.
    • Most AI tools run on models built by a handful of large labs and companies. Most people use them through apps, not directly.
    • AI depends on a physical system: internet connections, specialized chips, data centers, and electricity.
    • Data centers store data, run everyday apps, and, newest of all, train AI models.

    In short, artificial intelligence (AI) is “a broad term for computer systems that can perform tasks with human-like intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images, learning from data, reasoning, and making decisions” (Stanford HAI).

    Unlike traditional software, which follows rules written step by step by programmers, modern AI systems “learn” from data. They find patterns across millions or billions of examples and use those patterns to make predictions or responses in new situations. In some cases, they can be enabled to complete tasks with minimal human supervision.

    Before Now
    Specific AI tools were already being used daily in a variety of ways (e.g., Google search, spam filters, GPS, voice assistants). Flexible generative models (e.g., LLMs/ChatGPT) that create text, code, and media directly from user prompts, and are able to act autonomously.

    The core technology

    Most of today’s AI tools run on models. A model is essentially just very complex statistics. Computers (whether on your phone, an on-site server, or in a data center) use these models to respond to people’s requests. To do this, they draw on immense amounts of data to interpret a request and work out the most logical steps to complete a task.

    • Who builds them: Models are developed by AI research labs and large corporations, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft.
    • What they need: Building (or “training”) a model requires a massive amount of data, along with huge amounts of computing power and electricity.
    • How we use them: Most people never touch a model directly. Instead, they use an app (like ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, or a school tool like MagicSchool) that sends their request to a model running in a data center somewhere else.

    What can it do?

    Kind of work Examples
    Standard tasks Drafting emails, summarizing long documents, creating spreadsheets, taking meeting notes
    Research Producing research reports, analyzing data, answering questions about a large set of documents. Scientists and mathematicians are also using large language models to speed up research, such as inventing new drugs, solving fluid mechanics problems, or reading mammograms to detect cancer.
    Creative work Producing images and videos, or helping with key steps in an artist’s workflow that aren’t just producing the art itself (like brainstorming, editing, or captioning)

    What infrastructure does it take?

    AI is more than just the apps on our phones and computers. To make applications like Claude and ChatGPT possible, it requires a large physical system behind the scenes.

    Piece What it is Why it matters locally
    Internet The fiber-optic cables and networks that carry your request to a data center and bring the answer back Fast, reliable connections are one reason companies choose a location
    Chips Specialized computer chips are like the “brains” of AI. A single chip can perform trillions of calculations per second Making chips takes factories, water, and minerals. Oregon has a large chip industry
    Data centers Buildings full of computers (with chips) that process requests and send answers back to users They need land, water for cooling, and huge amounts of electricity
    Power The electricity that runs and cools the computers Data centers tend to consume a lot of electricity, which can affect the grid and power bills

    Data centers are not new; they have been the backbone of the internet for decades. They do three main jobs:

    1. Store and retrieve data (“cloud computing”). This is the most familiar use of data centers, and what the current AI industry is built on. Even before the AI industry took off, data centers were needed to store the data for websites, stream videos on sites like YouTube, and back up photos and email. Over the past few decades, more and more of our information has been stored in data centers.
    2. Run calculations for everyday apps (“inference”). Data centers have always done the computing behind everyday apps. When you search for something on Google, the algorithms that power the search run on a computer in a data center. Each time someone asks an AI chatbot a question, a data center does that work too.
    3. Train AI models. This is the newest use for data centers. Training a large model can take thousands of specialized chips running nonstop for weeks or months.

    What AI-related decisions are happening in Central Oregon?

    Key points

    • AI already shows up in local businesses, data centers, classrooms, policing, and government offices.
    • This Assembly focuses on decisions government is making about AI, and how the public can influence them.
    • These decisions come in three types: government use of AI, permissive planning, and restrictive regulations.

    AI is already part of daily life in Central Oregon, sometimes in ways that we know about, and sometimes in ways that are harder to see. It shows up in local businesses, in the region’s growing number of data centers, in classrooms, in policing, and inside government offices.

    What we are most focused on during this Assembly are the decisions that the government is making related to AI, and how the public can influence those decisions. For example, an issue like “how to manage AI in the classroom” involves school boards across the region creating new technology use policies, with some guidance from the state Department of Education. We found many examples of these decisions at various levels of government, including:

    • The City of Bend developing guidance for how city workers use AI, and figuring out which uses of AI are desired and beneficial for the public
    • Multiple school boards procuring new AI to support educational outcomes in the classroom
    • The City of Prineville discussing new data centers in its economic planning strategies, and how additional revenue from these projects should be used
    • Organizers in Bend turning out to shut down the use of AI-powered surveillance systems in their city
    • And many more

    We have broken these down into three types of decisions: what AI is used for, planning decisions, and restrictive regulations. As you think about the AI-related issues that matter most to you, try to identify where they fit in this map.

    Type What government is deciding Key opportunities Where the public usually fits in
    Uses of AI technology Whether and how government itself uses AI tools (for classroom support, public benefits, application review, etc.) Requests for qualifications, contracts, AI use policies Discussions around use policies may happen, but engagement on procurement decisions is rare
    Permissive planning Whether and where private AI investments (like data centers) can locate, and on what terms Economic plans, comprehensive plans, growth boundaries, permits, tax agreements Hearings on long-range plans and specific projects
    Restrictive regulations How to rein in possible harms from private industry Laws, ordinances, administrative rules, utility orders Agenda setting, advisory bodies, public hearings

    The following sections describe each of these types of decisions in more detail. Explore each one to learn more about who is involved in these decisions, what the rules are, and where the public could have a say.

    Government useProcurement and AI use policies.Planning and permissionsWhether, where, and on what terms projects like data centers can locate.RegulationsLaws, ordinances, and rules that rein in possible harms.

    Government use: procurement and AI use policies

    Key points

    • Government buys AI tools through requests for qualifications and contracts. Small purchases, like Bend’s Flock cameras, may skip public review entirely.
    • Public input on purchases is uncommon, for reasons like market fairness, workload, and technical expertise.
    • Oversight bodies and contract renewals give the public other chances to weigh in.
    • AI use policies come from the state, school districts, and city managers, often with little public input.
    Who’s involved
    The city manager, school boards, and other city staff
    What rules are already in place
    Public invitations to bid and requests for solicitation
    Potential impacts and tradeoffs
    Faster, greater public service capacity must be balanced against privacy and accuracy concerns
    Where the public could have a say
    Shaping procurement goals, taking part in evaluations, and giving feedback on technology impacts
    Case study
    Bend-La Pine School District’s AI use policy

    Government agencies are already using AI tools, mostly to help staff work faster. The rationale for the public sector to use these systems is similar to the private sector: increase efficiency and speed of transactions and lower the costs (Hodjick 2022).

    Procurement is the process the government uses to buy goods and services. Larger purchases are usually defined through a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) or similar request, which describes what the government needs; these documents are usually available online, before vendors apply and are selected. Final purchasing decisions are settled through a contract with the company providing the services.

    Here are some examples:

    Tool Who bought it Notes
    Microsoft Copilot City of Bend Only AI chatbot approved for city staff
    Flock Safety license plate cameras Bend Police Department Bought with grant funds; contract not renewed after public pushback
    MagicSchool AI Bend-La Pine Schools Procurement guided by state (ODE) guidelines

    Throughout these processes, transparency is generally required to preserve trust and accountability with the public. Secrecy in public contracting can lead to waste, corruption, and loss of public trust (OGP, The Costs of Secrecy). Bid documents are typically posted for the public on portals like oregonbids.com (see the City of Bend example). Small purchases may skip public review entirely, as staff can buy things under their own purchasing authority (this was the case with the Flock cameras). Some experts argue procurement rules should require more from AI companies, such as details of data qualities, model decisions, optimization techniques and processes when required by the public entity.

    Opportunities for public feedback during these processes (e.g., public comment, voting, and other public input) are generally uncommon, for some good reasons:

    • Keeping the market fair. Governments don’t want to give one supplier an unfair advantage, or force a private company to disclose information that would put it at a disadvantage compared to its competitors.
    • Workload. Opening every purchase to public input would overwhelm staff, taking time away from other important work.
    • Technical expertise. Many details of the services being bought require technical expertise that most residents (and even many officials) don’t have.

    On the other hand, governments can create oversight bodies to watch over certain kinds of purchases. Examples include public policing commissions, or Bend’s Human Rights and Equity Commission, which received updates on the Flock decision (City of Bend HREC minutes, Jan 13, 2026).

    After purchasing decisions are made, the public can still have influence. Contracts come up for renewal, and councils can review them. In Bend, public pressure led the city not to renew the Flock contract, and later to promise a council vote and public input before adding new license plate cameras from Axon (The Source).

    AI use policies set the rules for how government workers, school community members, and others may use AI to improve their work. This is another opportunity to shape how these technologies impact the lives of residents.

    • In education, many guidelines come down from higher levels of government. For example, the Oregon Department of Education created thorough guidelines for districts (ODE). Districts then write their own policies (see the Bend-La Pine case study).
    • In state government, agencies follow a statewide Responsible AI Usage Policy and an AI risk management framework. Public-facing AI tools must post a disclosure card (State uses, from Amy Paul).
    • In local government, policies like Bend’s are usually set by the city manager as administrative rules. The Bulletin’s editorial board said the public had no chance to weigh in on Bend’s policy (Central Oregon Decisions tracker).

    Planning and permissions

    Key points

    • Planning decides whether, where, and on what terms a community wants new development like data centers.
    • Oregon has 111 operating data centers, which used about 23% of the state’s retail electricity in 2025.
    • Planning departments often engage residents while shaping long-range plans; there are usually smaller chances once plans are being finalized.
    • Deals with large companies, like community benefit agreements and tax incentives, are usually negotiated privately, often under nondisclosure agreements.
    What does it govern
    Data centers, permits for power lines, land easements, and more
    Who’s involved
    Planning commissions, Economic Development for Central Oregon (EDCO), and the Central Oregon Intergovernmental Council (COIC) are involved in data center siting decisions
    What rules are already in place
    Oregon state laws govern community benefits in exchange for tax abatements, general plans guide land use, and most industrial siting decisions are handled through agreements between companies and cities
    Potential impacts and tradeoffs
    Attracting large industrial players (e.g., AI companies, data center operators) brings economic and community benefits, but also raises concerns about energy use, noise, and broader environmental impacts
    Where the public could have a say
    Comments on general plans, co-design opportunities, and input on community benefit agreements or how revenue is spent
    Case study
    Data centers in Prineville & La Pine

    In the local context, this is most relevant to data centers and other physical AI investments. The goal of these decisions is to figure out whether, where, and on what terms a community wants new development.

    At the state level, a first-of-its-kind report from ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia found the following:

    Measure Oregon today
    Operating data centers 111
    Planned or under construction 32 more
    Share of state’s retail electricity sales (2025) About 23%
    Projected share by 2030 31 to 32%
    Direct data center workers 2,630 (about 0.2% of the state workforce; 2,205 in Eastern Oregon)

    The state has recently put new rules in place to manage this growth. These include a pause on new enterprise-zone tax breaks for data centers (HB 4084, 2026), a separate electricity rate class for very large power users like data centers (the POWER Act, HB 3546, 2025), and a statewide Data Center Advisory Committee (Central Oregon Decisions tracker).

    Planning sets the long-term vision for a community’s economy and land, as well as policies that might encourage (or discourage) certain kinds of economic growth. This may include things like:

    • Comprehensive (general) plans set the overall vision and rules for land use in a city or county. These are often developed by the Planning Department of the city or county.
    • Economic Development Strategy (EDS): A regional economic plan developed by extragovernmental entities, like the Economic Development Corporation of Central Oregon or the Central Oregon Intergovernmental Council (COIC).
    • Economic Opportunities Analysis (EOA): Oregon’s land use rules require cities to plan for enough land and economic opportunities to support their expected growth over the next 20 years. Economic Development for Central Oregon (EDCO) helps local governments develop these analyses.
    • Enterprise development zones, where special tax breaks, regulatory relief, and other incentives might make it easier for larger corporations to bring labor, tax revenue, and more to the region.
    • Urban Growth Boundary (UGB) adjustments decide where a city can grow. In Oregon, a UGB expansion needs approval from both the city and the county.

    Before these plans are established: It is common practice for planning departments to do thorough community engagement when shaping up larger planning documents and strategies. This helps to align the plans for the city or county with the community’s vision for where they live, their values, the risks that they see, and more. The extent of engagement varies based on the entity involved and the type of planning document that they are producing:

    • EDCO engages residents in the region when it refreshes its Economic Development Strategy every three years.
    • The city of Arcata, CA engaged its residents in a lengthy community engagement process when creating its economic development plan (Arcata).
    • It is common for cities and counties to engage their residents in years-long engagement processes to develop their general plans, which include things like zoning decisions (which kinds of businesses are allowed to be where), investment priorities, transportation planning, and more.

    As the plans are actually developed, there are usually smaller opportunities for the public to weigh in. In some cases, committees or advisory boards might be established to help provide real-time feedback as the details of the planning documents are established. At the very least, most of these documents are officially adopted by the local governments, who may hold public meetings to discuss the details of the plans before they are officially voted on. In some cases, residents have organized petitions against certain aspects of a plan (e.g., urban growth boundaries in Prineville), which have motivated changes in the scope or details of planning decisions.

    Afterwards, both public and private entities use the plans to guide their decision-making. The city will often use these plans to guide its investments and industrial policies, and businesses, both local and large, often base their decisions on them too.

    While the public may have some opportunities for feedback in the earlier stages, decisions with larger corporations and developers are more likely to depend on private negotiations between the city or county and that private entity. These decisions might include things like:

    • Community Benefit Agreements (CBAs) are basically a way of saying, “You can come here on these conditions, to make sure you help our community thrive.” This might include everything from the corporation paying for essential infrastructure upgrades to providing grants for public schools, hiring locals for projects, and more. They are negotiated between the city or county and the corporation, and are made official through a contract. Some processes for determining community benefit agreements are more inclusive of the community than others.
    • Incentives: In order to bring Meta and Apple to Prineville, the city’s leaders waived property taxes for these corporations for 15 years.

    These discussions are usually much more private. Companies will often establish nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) with the city to protect their strategic plans, financials, and other information from giving their competitors a leg up; this also prevents the public from knowing many details about these plans before they are established. Recently, companies like Amazon have ended their practice of establishing NDAs after widespread public outcry. A key challenge is to figure out what information the public needs to know (and when) in order to guide decisions in their best interest.

    Regulations

    Key points

    • Regulations rein in possible harms from private industry: moratoriums, limits on tax breaks, electricity cost rules, and license plate reader rules.
    • The situation is moving fast. Gov. Kotek has set a 60-day deadline for the Legislature to pass data center rules.
    • Residents shape regulation through advocacy and agenda setting, public hearings, and advisory bodies.
    Who’s involved
    City councils, county commissions, and the State Legislature
    What rules are already in place
    Public comment processes are used during regulatory decisions
    Potential impacts and tradeoffs
    Regulations protect the public interest, but they have to balance effective oversight against rules that are too restrictive, given how uncertain emerging technology is
    Where the public could have a say
    Comments at council meetings, advocacy, and proposing community-informed policies

    Regulations help rein in the potential negative effects of private industry, and place guardrails and guidance around the actions of government, corporate, and individual actors to serve the public interest.

    Examples:

    • Data center moratoriums (temporary bans) at the local level, passed by city councils. Hillsboro, Salem, and Woodburn have passed them (OPB). At the state level, the Governor has paused data center permits until July 2027.
    • Limits on data center tax breaks passed by the Oregon Legislature (HB 4084, 2026).
    • Rules on electricity costs set by the Oregon PUC under the POWER Act (2025), so that very large users pay for the new power infrastructure they need.
    • License plate reader rules at the state level, which then shape local police purchasing decisions. Senate Bill 1516, signed in March 2026, added requirements like end-to-end encryption, and a statewide ban on Flock-type cameras has been proposed for 2027 (The Source; Central Oregon Decisions tracker).

    Governor Kotek recently announced a 60-day deadline for the state Legislature to pass more informed regulations (Oregon Capital Chronicle). This situation is evolving quickly, and more news is likely in the coming weeks and months.

    Public engagement in regulation:

    • Advocacy and agenda setting. Advocacy from residents is often what motivates new rules. This can include petitions, advocacy groups, and research that gathers evidence of potential harms. It usually runs through more organized, well-resourced organizations that have the time, capacity, and connections to reach public officials.
    • Public hearings at city council, the Legislature, or through online processes are also good opportunities to weigh in.
    • Public advisory bodies can be formed to help guide what and how to regulate. Oregon’s Data Center Advisory Committee is a good example. It heard testimony from local leaders (including Prineville’s) and took public comment on its preliminary findings through October 24, 2026. Newer innovations like civic assemblies can also serve as advisory bodies.

    What makes AI-related decisions different from other government decisions?

    Key points

    • In many ways, AI decisions resemble decisions about other major industries, like energy.
    • Speed: technology moves faster than the rules, and the scale of investment is larger than past booms like railroads and highways.
    • Private development: AI systems are hard to see inside, and well-funded companies can engage government in ways residents can’t.
    • Loss of agency: AI often automates human judgment, and many people feel they have little say.

    In some ways, AI-related decisions are not very different from other decisions government agencies make. It is generally helpful to compare AI to other major industries, like energy (oil, gas, hydropower, renewables). Like a new power plant or factory, a data center brings jobs and tax revenue but also uses land, water, and electricity. Local officials have pointed out that Prineville’s existing data centers are not AI data centers, and that many of the same land use and tax tools apply.

    However, it’s worth calling out a few things that make this industry different.

    Speed: technology moves faster than the rules

    The speed of technological progress outpaces our ability to regulate it. Researchers call this the Collingridge dilemma, named after a 1980 book on controlling technology. It describes a double bind: “Early on, intervention is possible but impacts are uncertain. Once impacts become clear, the technology is entrenched” (Wikipedia, summarizing The Social Control of Technology). This is closely related to the “pacing problem,” the idea that new technology increasingly outpaces laws and regulations.

    Content committee member Rachel Haakenson put it this way: regulation tends to follow adoption, which creates the feeling of a race.

    The speed and size of investment is larger than anything we’ve seen before. One Brookings analysis projects that investment in AI data center buildings, power systems, networks, and specialized chips will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032. That’s an average of 3.63% of U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) every year. “The projected buildout would be larger relative to the economy than the major U.S. canal, railroad, electrification, highway, and telecommunications investment booms,” writes the author, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of Columbia University (Brookings).

    Massive, speedy investment also means that local governments may feel they can’t afford to be “left behind” in the wave of technological progress and economic growth. For many, this feels like a pivotal moment. At the same time, content committee member Robin Hayakawa noted that community-facing AI in local government does not need to be rushed, and that residents should always be able to reach a real person.

    Private development: public input can be limited or outcompeted

    The “black box” challenge. It is hard to know exactly how AI systems work, what data they were (or were not) trained on, and why they give the answers they do.

    • Many layers between the community and the model. Most AI tools are provided through private service providers, who themselves depend on AI models built by a few very large companies (like Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft). This makes it difficult to change how the models behave to meet the specific needs or concerns of local residents.
    • It doesn’t have to be this way. Communities and governments can also use locally governed models or “open-weight” models, whose inner workings can be inspected and adjusted.
    • Some things can’t be taken back. Content committee member Marcio Nunes noted that institutional knowledge fed into shared AI systems can’t be “un-taught,” which raises questions about ownership and trust.

    Well-funded companies can engage governments in ways regular residents can’t. High investment in AI companies often means they have the time, budget, and skill to work with city and regional governments far more than everyday residents can. Companies like Waymo and Flock have invested heavily in public relations and government outreach. Flock, for example, spent $102,000 lobbying in Wisconsin alone in 2025, and has given campaign money to local officials whose agencies use its cameras (Wisconsin Examiner; Chicago Sun-Times). Playbooks for winning local approval are being developed in a way that feels notably different from earlier industrial revolutions.

    Communities are developing playbooks too. Data Center Watch describes local opposition groups as having “internalized an opposition playbook,” sharing tactics across 49 states (Data Center Watch).

    Loss of agency

    • The way AI systems are deployed often means automating human judgment: decisions once made by a person (a teacher, a clerk, a police officer) are now shaped or made by software.
    • Combined with the speed of development and the presence of well-financed private companies, many people feel a profound loss of agency with the arrival of the AI industry. In Oregon, about 60% of voters report negative feelings about AI (KLCC/OPB).

    Case studies

    Key points

    • Two real Central Oregon decisions show how the public’s role plays out in practice.
    • Each case looks at the decision, who had authority, the public’s role, competing views, and what happened afterward.

    The case studies below show how real AI-related decisions have played out in Central Oregon. For each one, we look at:

    • The decision: What was being decided?
    • Who had authority: Who made the final call?
    • The public’s role: When and where could the public influence it?
    • Competing views: What did different people think?
    • What happened afterward?
    Bend-La Pine School District’s AI use policyHow a school district shaped its AI rules with stakeholders, and what changed after a parent petition.Data centers in Prineville & La PineTwo Central Oregon communities, two very different outcomes when data centers came calling.

    Case study: Bend-La Pine School District’s AI use policy

    Key points

    • Bend-La Pine Schools stood out as one of the best local examples of thorough public engagement on AI.
    • Stakeholder feedback led the district to ban teachers from using AI plagiarism detectors.
    • A parent petition with more than 1,100 signatures led the board to review all classroom technology, and the Student Voice Council got a disclosure double standard fixed.
    • Lessons include meeting people where they are, reaching beyond the same few volunteers, and simplifying formal processes.

    Through our research, the Bend-La Pine School District stood out as a great local example of thorough public engagement on how AI is used.

    The decision
    How AI may be used in classrooms by teachers and students, and which AI tools (like MagicSchool) the district uses
    Who had authority
    The school board sets policy. The superintendent decides how the policy is carried out, through “administrative regulations” that don’t need board approval
    The public’s role
    Stakeholder groups, public comment periods, school board meetings, and petitions
    Competing views
    Many see AI as a useful tool for teachers and students. Some parents worry about screen time, privacy, and AI’s effect on learning
    What happened afterward
    The district changed its policy to ban AI plagiarism detectors. After a parent petition, the board ordered a district-wide review of all classroom technology

    The district has many structures for public engagement. It uses a very iterative process to get its policies right, plus forums for feedback with many different stakeholder groups:

    • Student Voice Council, an advisory body of representatives of the student body
    • Parent groups (PTAs)
    • Specific committees with parents and subject-matter experts (on technology, equity, and other topics) that help shape policy
    • Advocacy and equity coaches who listen to community concerns and report back to the district’s policy director
    • School board meetings and public comment periods

    As Karen Rush of Bend-La Pine Schools put it: “Our policies aren’t chiseled in stone. But the process is pretty clear.”

    Public engagement on AI:

    • Before: The State of Oregon produced guidelines for AI use in school districts, which shaped the district’s starting point (ODE). Opportunities for public feedback at this stage were fairly limited, but it motivated the school district to form its own use policies.
    • During: Bend-La Pine Schools engaged its stakeholder groups to shape its own policy. This included basic protections like student privacy and teacher discretion over AI use. Stakeholders raised concerns early on, for example that AI plagiarism detectors are unreliable and biased against students learning English as a second language. The district made a real change here: its policy now bans teachers from using AI plagiarism detectors.
    • After: Multiple points of public feedback pushed the district to make more changes:
      • A petition by Bend parents gathered over 1,100 signatures over concerns about AI and technology in classrooms, including MagicSchool. This led to community conversations and public comment, and in April 2026 the school board adopted a resolution to review all classroom technology and set grade-level technology standards (The Source; The Bulletin).
      • The Student Voice Council raised an issue they had with what they saw as a double standard: students were required to disclose their AI use, but teachers were not. This was amended in a later version of the district-wide use policy.

    Lessons and reflections:

    • Stakeholder groups are more siloed than the district would like. The district also relies on the same engaged people again and again, which leads to burnout.
    • Representation is hard. The district stretches from La Pine to Bend, and in-person meetings at the downtown Bend office are hard for rural families to attend. Student council members tend to be college-bound students, not a cross-section of all students.
    • It really matters to meet people where they are. Ideas include going into community spaces, using text messages, and collecting student feedback at lunch instead of through online forms.
    • Processes for public engagement are a little too complex and formal.
    • Limits on what the public can change: A completely “zero-tech” or “zero-AI” classroom isn’t realistic. Textbook publishers no longer print physical books, and state tests are now digital. Parents have also raised worries about voice-recognition software in state testing.

    Case study: Data centers in Prineville & La Pine

    Key points

    • Prineville welcomed data centers during an economic crisis, with little public debate. Their tax breaks begin expiring in 2027.
    • Crook County’s unemployment fell from nearly 20% to about 6%, but residents are now divided about the data centers.
    • La Pine faced a proposal during a time of strong public skepticism. Residents organized quickly, and the council rejected the sale unanimously.
    • Both decisions were made by city councils, but the public’s role was very different.

    Neither of these cases involves a large “AI data center” of the newest kind; Prineville’s existing data centers were built mostly for cloud computing, and La Pine’s proposal was mainly for cryptocurrency mining. However, they are good examples of how communities make decisions about data centers, and they show two very different outcomes.

    Prineville

    The decision
    Whether to welcome large data centers, and on what terms (tax breaks, land, water, infrastructure)
    Who had authority
    City of Prineville and Crook County (land use and enterprise zone tax deals), with help from EDCO
    The public’s role
    Council and county meetings where the deals were approved. Little proactive community engagement
    Competing views
    Many credit the data centers with saving the local economy. Others say they raised the cost of living, changed the small-town feel, and use too much land, water, and power
    What happened afterward
    Tax breaks begin expiring in 2027. The city now says it wants more from future deals

    In the city’s own words, Prineville was “dying on the vine” following the housing crash and didn’t have other options knocking on its door (Marketplace). When Meta first approached the city, the city pursued a number of economic arrangements to make sure the data centers would benefit the community, including franchise fees on electricity (about $1 million per month today) and company-funded water storage and wastewater projects (Marketplace).

    Timeline:

    1. 2002An Economic Opportunities Assessment laid out several options for industrial development.
    2. 2008 to 2010The housing crisis and Great Recession brought the city to its knees. The timber industry was dying, and county unemployment approached 20% (Marketplace).
    3. Late 2009 to 2010A then-secret “well-funded, well-known company” negotiated to build in Prineville’s enterprise zone (Data Center Knowledge). Facebook finalized the deal and broke ground in 2010.
    4. 2011 onwardFacebook’s first data center opened in 2011. Apple followed. Both received 15-year property tax breaks through Oregon’s rural enterprise zone program. Each new building got its own deal (Marketplace).
    5. 2026Prineville’s new Economic Opportunities Analysis lists data centers as a possible future investment, citing past benefits. City leaders told the state they favor future data centers but will not offer more full tax breaks (Central Oregon Decisions tracker).
    6. 2027 to 2035The data centers’ tax breaks expire one building at a time. Meta’s tax bill is expected to jump from about $178,000 to $4 million in the first year, more than a quarter of the county’s property tax receipts (Marketplace).

    Despite the apparent success, there was not much public engagement:

    • The work was led mainly by the city’s economic development department, EDCO, and consultants.
    • There was little public pushback at the time. This highlights how today feels different from earlier waves of investment, when data centers served uses people accepted more readily (cloud storage, video streaming, recommendation algorithms).
    • Today, residents are more divided. Some credit the data centers for good jobs. Others say the facilities raised the cost of living, light up the night sky, and should be shared with other communities rather than concentrated in one place.

    Now, the city says it is in a position to demand more from AI companies, including and beyond Meta (The Source). The 2026 economic plan includes data centers as a potential investment, citing the benefits they brought before. It found the city is out of large industrial sites and needs about 755 more acres (Central Oregon Decisions tracker).

    However, the biggest fight in this recent planning review wasn’t about data centers. It was about expanding the urban growth boundary for a biomass power plant on what had been farmland. Most city and county officials pointed out that the city’s growth has depended on steady, strategic boundary adjustments, while residents argued that converting farmland goes against their community’s values. The city later resumed its plan without fully addressing the biomass project or urban growth boundary issue.

    La Pine

    In May 2026, the La Pine City Council unanimously rejected a proposed land sale of approximately 20 acres in the La Pine Industrial Park to Boxminer.io for a 20-megawatt data center. Although the developer promised local jobs without inflating power bills or water usage, residents expressed strong opposition due to concerns over noise, community impacts, and potential strains on the rural power grid and water resources, leading to the decision following public outcry.

    The decision
    Whether to sell about 20 acres in the La Pine Industrial Park to Boxminer.io for a 20-megawatt data center
    Who had authority
    La Pine City Council
    The public’s role
    Public comment at council meetings; petitions
    Competing views
    The developer promised jobs and no excessive water use or higher power bills. Residents worried about the power grid, water, noise, and community effects
    What happened afterward
    The council rejected the sale unanimously on May 27, 2026

    Timeline of public engagement:

    • Before: In March 2026, the La Pine City Council voted to start the process of selling the land and asked city staff to learn more about the proposal (The Source). The local economic development board recommended the project.
    • During: Nearly 100 residents showed up to a May 13 council meeting, even though the data center wasn’t on the agenda (KTVZ). Many residents were upset they hadn’t been notified about the March vote (The Source). The council heard nearly five hours of public comment that month, mostly against the project. Residents worried about the fragile rural power grid.
      • The 20-megawatt facility would use about 15 times the electricity used by all the households in a city La Pine’s size (OPB).
      • The developer promised “up to” 200 jobs, but the city manager’s report estimated it might be closer to five (The Source).
    • After: The council voted unanimously to reject the sale on May 27, 2026. “We do listen to you because we live here as well,” the council president told the crowd (The Source).

    Why “public engagement”?

    Key points

    • About 266,000 people live in Crook, Deschutes, and Jefferson counties, and state and local government shapes nearly every part of daily life, from land and zoning to schools and public health.
    • People in Oregon have the right to give input on decisions that affect them, through elections and other ways to weigh in on specific decisions.
    • Hearings, comment periods, surveys, ballot measures, and boards and commissions are some of those ways.
    • This section describes how engagement works today. What counts as “good” engagement is left to delegates.

    Note: This section describes how engagement works today, and broadly what it is meant to achieve. It does not define what “good” engagement means; that is left to delegates.

    About 266,000 people live in Crook, Deschutes, and Jefferson counties, and nearly every part of their daily lives is shaped by state and local government. (Census, July 2025 estimates: Deschutes, Crook, Jefferson.) This includes decisions about how our land and natural resources are managed, what kind of businesses are allowed to be here and where (zoning), how our schools are managed, how public health is protected, and much more. Each of these is managed by one or more departments at the city, county, and state levels (or sometimes federal, in the case of certain public lands).

    People who live in Oregon have the right and the opportunity to provide input into the decisions that affect them. We affect some of those decisions through electing representatives, but we also have other means to weigh in on specific decisions.

    Effective public engagement helps ensure that public sector decisions are informed not only by technical expertise, but also by the knowledge, values, priorities, and personal experiences of the people who will be affected by those decisions and whose tax dollars support them.

    Examples of formal public engagement in state and local decisions include:

    • State legislative hearings, and city council and county commission meetings that are open to the public and invite public comment
    • Town halls on specific topics
    • Surveys
    • Public comment periods when local or state rules are being drafted
    • Public meetings organized by local or state elected officials
    • Public hearings required by state and local law for local legislation and quasi-judicial land use applications (for example, code updates, conditional use permits, and zone changes)
    • Initiatives and referenda, through which citizens and advocacy groups can place items on the ballot for the public to approve or deny
    • Boards and commissions, where citizens may be appointed
    • And, of course, elections

    Who gets involved in public decisions?

    Key points

    • Government makes the final decision, but residents, organized groups, advocacy groups, businesses, and public-private coordinators all take part.
    • Residents who organize tend to have more influence, because officials see them as speaking for a broader group.
    • Decisions involving companies, like software contracts and data center deals, are often less visible to the public.
    • EDCO says early recruitment is kept confidential for good reasons, and that public input comes through elected officials, its strategy meetings, and public votes on long-term incentives.

    Our state and local governments may be responsible for making the final decisions, but many groups take part in public decisions. Each plays a different role.

    Who What they do Central Oregon examples
    Government Makes and carries out decisions. State decisions often set the rules that local governments must follow. State agencies, county commissions, city councils, school boards, special districts, public advisory commissions made up of members of the public
    Individuals Every resident has the right to take part in local decisions, both through formal means (public meetings, comment periods, public hearings, etc.) and informal means (organizing petitions, direct actions, etc.). Speaking at a council meeting, emailing a commissioner, etc.
    Organized residents When residents organize, officials tend to see them as speaking for a broader group, not just one person.
    Advocacy groups Speak for a cause or community. They often follow issues closely and comment on behalf of members, or file lawsuits. Central Oregon LandWatch, The Environmental Center, 1000 Friends of Oregon, Oregon Rural Action, Bend Privacy Alliance, etc.
    Businesses and business groups Often have significant sway. They may sell services to government, seek incentives to locate here, or hire lobbyists to advocate on their behalf. Local businesses, AI companies, real estate developers or agents
    Public-private coordinators Separate organizations that develop strategies for the development of the region and coordinate across the public and private spheres. Organizations like EDCO may also be involved in recruiting, keeping, and supporting businesses that move to the region. Economic Development for Central Oregon, Central Oregon Intergovernmental Council

    Public-private negotiations

    Many government decisions related to AI in particular involve companies that are selling services to the government (for example, MagicSchool AI selling its software to local school districts), or working with the government to develop their operations in the area (for example, data center developments). Compared to decisions that go through local councils or planning commissions, these are often less visible to the public.

    On the other hand, there could also be good reasons for these private dealings to remain private. Economic Development for Central Oregon (EDCO) says early recruitment is often kept confidential to protect companies’ competitive information and workers. It calls these confidentiality agreements a real limit, not bad faith, though it often means the public learns of a project after major terms are set. EDCO believes the appropriate places for public input are elected officials, its three-year community strategy meetings, and public votes on long-term incentives.

    How and when can the public get involved?

    Key points

    • Engagement can happen before a decision, while it’s being made, and after it takes effect.
    • The floor: state and local law require notice before meetings, comment during them, and boards and commissions residents can serve on. Some decisions still happen out of public view.
    • The ceiling: officials can go further, with options like longer notice, civic assemblies, and oversight committees.
    • Having a chance to engage isn’t the same as being able to use it. Schedules, language, distance, internet access, and trust all get in the way.

    Engagement can happen before the government makes a decision, while it is being made, and after it takes effect. At each stage, there are important opportunities for residents, corporations, and others outside the government to shape the decisions to meet their interests.

    Stage Why Common examples
    Before (notice, education) Opportunities to learn about the issue and its impacts, so that later engagement is well-informed and impactful Public notices, mailing lists, staff reports, explainers, educational sessions, city and county email lists, etc.
    During (feedback, deliberation) Offering feedback on what the proposed decisions do well and poorly, so that they can be improved before they are implemented Public comment during council meetings, advisory committees, budget hearings
    After (accountability, appeals) Checking in to make sure that the implemented policy is doing what it was intended to do, with reasonable resources Regular reporting on results, audits, appeals, oversight bodies, lawsuits, etc.

    The floor: what is the minimum public engagement that the government has to support?

    There are three main ways the public is required to be included under state and local law: public notices ahead of meetings, comments during public meetings, and the many boards and commissions that members of the public can serve on. This is what we call the “floor” of public engagement, but public agencies and officials can always choose to do more.

    Opportunity Stage What the law requires
    Notices Before Public meetings need advance notice: at least 48 hours for regular meetings and 24 hours for special ones. Property owners near a land use decision must get mailed notice, and state agencies must publish notice at least 21 days before adopting rules. (ORS 197.763, ORS 183.335)
    Public comment During Public meetings that take in-person testimony must also allow remote testimony. Public comment is required at hearings for land use cases, local budget decisions, state rule changes, and utility rate or water right proceedings. Enterprise zone tax agreements longer than three years need resolutions adopted at public meetings. (Oregon Public Meetings Law)
    Boards and commissions During and/or after These groups meet regularly to provide public oversight and make decisions about certain parts of government. For example, under Oregon’s Local Budget Law, local governments must have citizen budget committees made up of appointed members of the public and city or county councilors. Planning commissions work in a similar way, reviewing and approving land use proposals (Statewide Planning Goal 1). At the state level, the Governor appoints members to more than 265 state boards and commissions, and electric cooperatives hold member-elected board elections.

    There are also a few notable places where decisions can move out of public view. These practices aren’t necessarily meant to shut the public out. They let the government carry out its work efficiently.

    • Legislative versus executive decisions. Councils, commissions, and the Legislature set policy in public meetings, where the public can engage more directly. Executive offices and government staff then carry out their duties under those policies, and can make decisions or set priorities with little public review. Public review of every single government decision would quickly grind public service to a halt. Instead, most government activity can be looked into through meeting records, public records requests, and other means.
      • In Prineville, community input on enterprise zone agreements came through elected officials (the mayor, city council, and county commissioners), with no separate public process.
    • By-right zoning. Many land use decisions go through a planning commission before they are final, but some uses are allowed “outright” or “by right,” meaning they skip that review. This is also meant for efficiency, when a use is considered safe and already fits what the city or county wants to develop. In Prineville, for example, data centers are allowed outright in the industrial park on the rim of the city, where utilities have already been upgraded to support them.
    • Nondisclosure agreements (NDAs). Larger businesses often sign NDAs that keep the details of their negotiations and business private unless they choose to share them.
      • For data centers in particular, this may be changing. In October 2026, Amazon said it no longer uses NDAs with the government agencies it works with on its projects, following a similar move by Microsoft. This could give the public earlier notice before major projects come to town, though Amazon’s change applies only going forward. (TechCrunch, Oct 3, 2026)

    The ceiling: where could the public have more involvement?

    The “ceiling” is how much power the public could have, beyond what the law requires. Depending on funding and interest, public officials can create more opportunities for meaningful public engagement.

    Who gets to take part? Having a chance to engage is not the same as being able to use it. Meetings may happen during working hours, go on for hours, or follow rules that limit what people can say. Barriers in Central Oregon include language and interpretation, disability access, work and caregiving schedules, distance and transportation, internet access, and trust in institutions. These look different across ages: a working parent, a retiree, and a high school student each face different hurdles. Two questions to keep in mind for every stage: who is missing, and who keeps getting asked?

    What could this look like? Many of the ideas above the floor draw on the principles of good deliberation:

    • Representative. The people taking part reflect the whole community, not just those with the time to show up. Civic assemblies do this by randomly selecting participants, and stipends, childcare, and interpretation help more people say yes.
    • Informed. Participants get time and balanced information to understand an issue before weighing in. Examples include briefing materials, site visits, and Q&A sessions with experts from different sides.
    • Dialogic. People talk with each other and with decision-makers, not just at them. A facilitated small-group discussion with planning staff allows back-and-forth that a three-minute comment slot doesn’t.

    Before, during, and after

    The next few sections give you more to consider for each stage of public engagement: before, during, and after decisions are made. Click on the links below to explore.

    Before a decisionNotice, information, and due diligence.During a decisionFeedback and deliberation.After a decisionAccountability and appeal.

    Before a decision: notice, information, due diligence

    Key points

    • Advance notice: people need to hear about decisions early enough to contribute. Oregon law requires meeting notices and mailed notices for many land use hearings, but renters, rural residents, and people farther away can be missed.
    • Information: accurate, balanced information helps people push for what helps and against real harms. Misinformation can get in the way, and officials can counter it by sharing accurate data early.
    • Due diligence: decision-makers need both the facts and a sense of what the public wants, ideally gathered in the open.

    Advance notice

    People need to hear about decisions that matter to them early enough to contribute.

    Why it matters. Simply put, you can’t weigh in on something you don’t know about. When people are left out, the government can make decisions that accidentally harm them, and trust drops, which makes compromise harder later. Local leaders said people are often brought in only after a decision is mostly made.

    “I think it’s important to have the community engagement piece far enough in advance from the organizational standpoint, the decision making standpoint, that decisions aren’t already made. It has to be still in the point where you can adjust strategies and not even really change the plan.”

    Rachel Haakenson, NeighborImpact

    What it looks like.

    • Meeting notices. Oregon’s Public Meetings Law requires notice of every meeting of a governing body: at least 48 hours ahead for regular meetings and 24 hours for special ones. Notices must list the date, time, place, how to join online, and the main topics.
    • Mailing lists. Many local governments let you sign up to get public notices and agendas by email (e.g., Crook County and the City of Prineville).
    • Land use notices. By law, cities and counties must mail notice at least 20 days ahead to nearby property owners for many land use decisions and public hearings: within 100 feet inside an urban growth boundary, 250 feet outside one, and 750 feet in farm or forest zones. Renters and people farther away may not get a letter. (ORS 197.763)

    Challenges. “Neighbor notice” of specific land use applications goes only to landowners within a few hundred feet of the proposed project. In rural areas, that can amount to very few people.

    Neighbor notices can also be hard to understand, because they rely on legal and land use jargon. State and local rules require notice of certain public hearings to be posted in the newspaper, but newspaper circulation is falling, and few Central Oregonians rely on the classified section of the local paper for news about local government.

    Information

    People need accurate, balanced information to take part in a meaningful way.

    Why it matters. Well-informed people can advocate for what will truly help them and against real harms. This includes learning about the topic itself (for example, the positive and negative impacts of using AI in the classroom), what decision is being made, who makes it, and on what timeline.

    On the other hand, misinformation can be a significant barrier to productive engagement. Multiple public officials in the region noted that they had seen misinformation about the impacts of AI-powered technologies, data centers, and more influence how people reacted to proposals. While they are not the source of misinformation, local governments and elected officials can counter it by proactively reaching out to residents and making sure accurate, transparent data is widely available.

    “Central Oregon has massive disparities in AI literacy. We need to help get everyone up to speed on the risks and opportunities AI poses to our communities.”

    Open Poll participant. 67% of participants agreed.

    “There needs to be more education on AI for the general public before many of these statements can be addressed. …no way to know if what I am reading/seeing is real or AI so I don’t trust it anymore.”

    Open Poll participant. 85% agreed.

    Adam Young pointed to a local claim that Ochoco Reservoir is low because of data centers as a reason for myth-versus-fact resources.

    What it looks like.

    • Accessible, balanced educational materials that explain the nature of the decisions being made, pros and cons, and more
    • Opportunities to sit down with public officials who are responsible for the decision
    • Funding local news and information distributors
    • Asking specific questions. Instead of only asking “data center or no data center,” Adam Young suggested asking where it would go and what its effects would be on the environment, light, and noise.
    • Learning from places that have faced similar problems

    Challenges. Good information often has to be pulled from many sources, and gathering it can be time intensive. People may not already agree on which details are important, or even what the truth of a matter is.

    Depending on the decision and any confidentiality limits, there may not be enough time or information for the general public to learn the nuances and the potential pros and cons of an issue. Passionate advocacy based on an incomplete or incorrect understanding can lead to worse decisions. It can also break down trust on both sides, which can color discussions well into the future.

    It is generally hard to expect people to dig into heavy, technical issues unless it is their job to understand them. This leaves residents relying on elected and appointed officials. In other places, public commissions of everyday residents have taken many months or even years to understand the impacts.

    Due diligence

    Decision-makers need good information from all sides, and they need to weigh the possible effects on the community.

    Why it matters. Public officials are expected to explain their decisions, justify how public money was used, and report on results. Knowing they will be expected to do so reinforces the importance of careful decision-making and stewardship of public funds, as well as responsiveness to the people they serve.

    What it looks like. Officials often ask for reports, briefings, and expert advice, and staff help produce them and connect officials with experts. This work has two parts: the facts (what is actually happening?) and public preferences (what do people actually want?). Ideally, this information gathering is transparent to the public, so that residents and advocates can call out potential gaps or draw their own conclusions.

    As a local example, the City of Prineville’s planning department says it treats data centers like any large industrial project: study the demand, check whether there is enough capacity, then negotiate development agreements and incentives.

    During a decision: feedback and deliberation

    Key points

    • Feedback lets the public weigh in before a policy is final, through comment periods, hearings, surveys, and listening sessions.
    • Local examples show feedback changing outcomes, from Bend-La Pine’s classroom AI rules to new transit service in Madras and Bend.
    • Comment processes often favor the most motivated voices, and engagement works best when it focuses on what can actually change.
    • Intermediary groups like NeighborImpact and Oregon’s Kitchen Table often have more room than government to reach people.
    • Deliberation, as in a civic assembly, asks residents to weigh tradeoffs together. Doing it well takes time, money, and skilled facilitation.

    Feedback

    Members of the public get a chance to weigh in on policies before they are final.

    Why it matters. Feedback is a chance for members of the public to share why a proposed policy or plan will or will not work for their community. They can offer data, personal experience, professional expertise, preferences, and community needs, to help plans meet the needs and values of more people. It is also a chance for public officials to explain what they are considering and why.

    What it looks like. Spaces for public feedback look different for different government bodies. Below are a few examples from formal and informal public bodies.

    Who What they did What changed
    Bend-La Pine Schools Board policy goes through required public comment. Parent and student voice councils also give input. The classroom chatbot lost its human-like persona and now flags emotional conversations to teachers. Adults now disclose AI use in grading. Teachers may not use AI plagiarism-detection tools on English-learner students.
    NeighborImpact For its biennial plan, surveys about problems (not proposed solutions) were distributed to those receiving services, with listening sessions in every city plus online and Spanish-language sessions. (NeighborImpact is not a government entity, but it faces similar challenges, and its experience can help inform government practices.) Decision-makers hear residents directly, and are more likely to prioritize what they heard.
    Cascades East Transit Spanish-language survey of Madras residents with the Latino Community Association, under an ODOT grant. Surveys and fare data led to 15-minute service on Third Street and a planned microtransit pilot in south Bend.

    Intermediary organizations like NeighborImpact, COCAP, and Oregon’s Kitchen Table help connect the community with decision-makers. They often have more room to maneuver than government: engagement is their main focus, they have the training, and they don’t have to work within the same rules and priorities that can hamstring government agencies.

    Challenges.

    • Who is heard. Good feedback reflects the whole community, not just a few loud voices or tokenized people. But comment processes often favor the most motivated people, professionals, and interested parties with their own goals and the time, capacity, and training to do it effectively. Creating effective spaces for public consultation takes funding and training many departments don’t have, or haven’t set aside for that purpose.
    • What to engage them on. Some decisions are already fixed by law, so asking the public about them is just box-checking. Engagement works best when it focuses on what can actually change.

    Deliberation

    The public can be invited to discuss and weigh the tradeoffs of a decision together.

    Why it matters. Making good decisions requires people not only to gather good information, but to talk through the values they hold and the tradeoffs between different options. Inside a government body, deliberation happens all the time: councils and boards debate before they vote. The public is rarely asked to do this to inform policies, but when it is done well, it can produce decisions that most residents support. Wendy Willis of Oregon’s Kitchen Table put it this way: when people must decide together, “the incentives are problem-solving incentives rather than [political] incentives.”

    What it looks like. The many boards and commissions across Central Oregon have elements of deliberation: residents who aren’t elected officials discuss public issues together and make decisions. But these conversations involve only a small group of people, not the wider public. And when the public is brought in for things like public comment, there is rarely room for two-way conversation between residents or with their representatives.

    The gold standard is deliberation that is inclusive, representative, informed, and conversational: many different kinds of affected people talking and considering each other’s reasons for what they believe. Juries are the most common example of public deliberation in practice, where a randomly selected group of residents learns about an issue and makes recommendations together. But there are many other examples:

    • Deschutes County formed a civic assembly on youth homelessness in fall 2025 that identified 22 actionable recommendations.
    • Oregon’s Citizens’ Initiative Review brings together a random panel of voters to study a ballot measure and write a statement for the voters’ pamphlet summarizing their support (or lack of it) and their reasoning.
    • Mosier, Oregon. After a train derailment, Oregon’s Kitchen Table ran a quick community conversation so the town knew what residents wanted before negotiating with the railroad.

    Challenges.

    • Doing deliberation well takes a lot of time and money. Recruitment of a representative group is especially challenging for the reasons above; the people who are most likely to show up are often those with more privilege in one way or another (socioeconomic status, English-speaking, etc.). Overcoming this takes a lot of time and money, which can quickly exhaust both participants and government staff.
    • Lack of training. Running a good meeting (one that tries to achieve a balance of voices, navigate conflict, etc.) often requires experienced facilitators, who can be hard to find and expensive to hire.

    After a decision: accountability and appeal

    Key points

    • Accountability means reporting results, justifying spending, and closing the loop with the people who gave input.
    • Oregon expects to publish a list of state AI uses, and public-facing state AI must offer a way to give feedback.
    • Ways to challenge a decision include school board appeals, the Land Use Board of Appeals, public meeting grievances, ballot measures, and lawsuits.
    • In land use appeals, an issue usually must be raised at the local hearing first, or it can’t be raised on appeal.

    Accountability

    The government shares what happened after a policy takes effect, checks that it was a good use of public money, and is ready to change course if needed.

    Why it matters. Accountability means public officials, through open processes, explain their decisions, justify how public money was used, report on results, and take responsibility for how things turned out. At the very least, it means closing the loop with the people who gave input. Kathi Barguil said institutions often lose people at this step: they ask for ideas, then never say how the input was used or why it wasn’t. “Community members want to know that the time that they put in mattered.”

    What it looks like.

    • Feedback requirements for technologies. A public list of state AI uses is expected by mid-2027, along with an annual report to the Governor and an AI adoption plan from each agency. Public-facing AI must have a way for users to give feedback, with review and escalation.
    • Addressing concerns. The Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development (DLCD) developed an Offshore Wind Energy Roadmap setting standards for offshore wind development. The process involved extensive public review and input from a multi-stakeholder Roundtable assembled in 2024. In July 2026, DLCD published the final Roadmap alongside a detailed document of responses to public comments, showing how community feedback was considered and worked into the final standards.
    • Audits. The Oregon Secretary of State’s Audits Division reviews how state agencies spend money and whether programs work, and publishes its findings.

    Appeal

    If a decision or policy isn’t working, or wasn’t made properly, the public should have ways to challenge it.

    Why it matters. No one can predict exactly how a policy will turn out once it is in place. Giving the public ways to appeal decisions lets us improve policies so that potential harms can be avoided.

    What it looks like.

    • School decisions. In Bend-La Pine, a concern goes first to the school, then to the superintendent’s office, then to the school board, which decides whether an action followed policy.
    • Land use decisions can be appealed to the Land Use Board of Appeals (LUBA). One catch: an issue usually must be raised at the local hearing, or it can’t be raised on appeal. This applies only to quasi-judicial and legislative land use decisions, but most land use decisions involving data centers or infrastructure fall into these categories.
    • Public meeting violations. Anyone can file a written grievance with the public body within 30 days; the body has 21 days to respond. If it doesn’t fix the problem, the person can complain to the Oregon Government Ethics Commission. Courts can also void decisions made in an unlawful meeting.
    • Pushing for proper process. Oregon Housing and Community Services emailed a handbook change barring funded organizations from using AI, “effective immediately.” NeighborImpact argued that enforceable guidance must go through rulemaking with public comment, and the change is now on hold.
    • Ballot measures. Oregon voters can refer laws and many local decisions to the ballot, or propose their own through an initiative.
    • Lawsuits. Individuals and advocacy groups can go to court to challenge decisions, enforce public records laws, or block government actions that violate statutory or constitutional rights.

    What tradeoffs need to be considered to create wise public policy?

    Key points

    • Creating policy means weighing goals that pull against each other.
    • Four tradeoffs to think about: cost and attention, expertise, point in the process, and level of influence.

    Creating policy means weighing goals that pull against each other. Here are a few questions to stimulate your thinking.

    • Cost and attention. Demanding thorough, deliberative public engagement on every single issue would quickly sap the attention that public administrators have to do their jobs and cost a lot of money. Where should the extra effort be applied, or how do you strike that balance?
    • Expertise. Many decisions related to AI require specialized knowledge to make an informed decision, whether related to the technology itself, administrative workings, economics, or otherwise. What are you okay with leaving to experts, and where do you want the voices of everyday people to take precedence? How can these things work well together?
    • Point in the process. At which points would you like to see more public engagement in local decisions regarding AI? When in a project’s life could public input considerably change the decisions that are made?
    • Level of Influence. Some would argue that we elect our representatives for a reason, and we should leave them to do their jobs. And giving residents direct control / influence over any public matters comes with its own risks. What kind of decisions should the public be able to participate in, and how much decision-making power should they have (from purely advisory to making it law)?

    How have other places dealt with similar challenges?

    Key points

    • AI decisions are complex, opaque, and high stakes, but other places have faced problems with similar traits.
    • Three short case studies show what people put in place, what worked, and what didn’t.

    As discussed in the previous section, decisions related to AI in the public sector face a number of unique challenges: the underlying technology is complex and often opaque, and the impacts are likely huge but difficult to pin down because the phenomenon is so new. Even still, many cities and counties across the country have dealt with similar challenges and found ways to involve the public in meaningful ways. These examples are not all related to artificial intelligence, but reflect many of the same characteristics (complex, uncertain, high stakes) in one way or another.

    Each short case study covers:

    • Some basic information about the circumstances
    • What the people implemented
    • What worked well, and what didn’t
    Loudoun County shifts away from by-right approval of data centersAfter two decades of courting the industry, the Virginia county with the world’s largest concentration of data centers changed its zoning rules so that every new data center must go through public hearings and a vote by elected officials, rather than a staff-level sign-off.The Hanford Advisory Board on nuclear wasteAfter four decades of plutonium production tainted the Columbia River watershed, a 37-person board representing different sectors of Washington and Oregon was assembled to present consensus-based recommendations to federal departments on how to clean it up.Oakland’s Privacy Commission on surveillance technologiesWhen residents learned the city planned to turn a port security system into a citywide surveillance hub, a coalition of residents, community groups, and privacy advocates pushed the city to scale it back, and won a standing citizen commission that reviews every surveillance technology the city wants to use before the City Council decides.

    More examples being researched

    • San Jose’s participatory algorithmic auditing: residents took part in evaluating a city algorithmic system, using a value-sensitive design approach.
